newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's hryvnia firms after central bank support.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's hryvnia firms after central bank support.

text.p: Ukraine's new hryvnia currency firmed on the interbank market on Wednesday, and the central bank, which has been supporting the currency strongly in recent days, was now able to buy dollars on the market, dealers said.
But the short-term outlook for the currency, introduced at the start of September, is uncertain, dealers said.
"It's hard to say what will happen by the end of the week, a rise or fall," said Yuri Krut of Banka Ukraina. "On the one hand banks have money, but the National Bank will probably hold the rate."
National Bank Chairman Viktor Yushchenko said on Monday the central bank would tighten currency trading rules to limit speculation.
He was talking after the hryvnia, which had been unchanged at 1.760 to the dollar since its introduction on September 2, slipped to 1.769 on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange.
On Tuesday it edged up to 1.768 on the exchange, and was quoted at 1.7680 on the domestic interbank market after 1.7740/7770 on Monday.
In trading outside Ukraine, the hyrvnia rose to 1.7730 from 1.7830/7900.
"Yesterday it was still hard to buy currency on the interbank market, but today you can without any problems," said Sergei Ponomarenko of Pravex Bank.
Dealers said the National Bank had been buying dollars at 1.7700 hryvnia, and Ponomarenko said rates could stabilise around this level.
Banka Ukraina's Krut said some bids to buy dollars had been withdrawn at the currency exchange following the National Bank's warning.

Dealers said the central bank would be able to influence the rate on the currency exchange and domestic market, but the hryvnia's behaviour on the external market, such as Moscow and Riga, could be decisive.

"The National Bank is able to close the difference between demand and offer on the exchange, but if a big difference opens up between rates on the domestic and non-resident markets, as happened last week, then foreign currency will start to leak out of various holes from Ukraine catastrophically," said Pravex's Ponomarenko.

Bankers said the introduction of the hryvnia last month, and the current withdrawal of the temporary karbovanets currency which it replaced, may have lead to a one-off technical jump in money supply, making it harder for the central bank to regulate the system.
